value.body: A radiology technologist positions patients and operates X-ray, CT, MRI and other imaging equipment to produce the images a radiologist reports on. Employers include hospitals, diagnostic imaging centres and diagnostic chains. A day involves preparing patients, choosing scan settings, taking images safely and managing them on the hospital's imaging systems.

items.label: Typical entry
items.note: Diploma courses are a shorter route

items.label: Radiation safety
items.value: AERB rules apply to X-ray and CT units

items.label: Common tools
items.value: X-ray, CT and MRI scanners; PACS image systems

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Class 12 with Physics, Chemistry and Biology, then a B.Sc in Radiology and Imaging Technology with an internship. Freshers usually start as radiographers or X-ray technicians and rotate across scan types; government posts are filled through recruitment exams.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Operating X-ray, CT and MRI consoles
Radiation protection and MRI safety checks
Checking image quality and managing images on PACS

value.title: At a glance
items: Specialising in CT, MRI or interventional radiology is a common next step.
Shift work, including nights, is common in hospital imaging units.
Some move into application specialist roles with imaging equipment makers.
